q: Displacement of a body is best described as:
o: The total length of the path followed by the body
The straight-line change in position from the initial to the final point, with direction
The total length of the path divided by the time taken
The shortest distance between two points, with no direction
x: Displacement is a vector: the change in position, drawn as a straight line from start to finish with a direction. The total path length is distance, a scalar.

q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s along a straight road. Using its average velocity, the distance it covers in this time is:
x: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (0 + 20) ÷ 2 = 10 m s⁻¹, so distance = 10 × 10 = 100 m. 200 m wrongly uses the final velocity for the whole time.

q: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the law of:
x: The first law states that a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a net force acts; this tendency is inertia, so it is called the law of inertia.

q: The law of conservation of linear momentum applies to a system of bodies when:
o: The bodies move with constant speed
Only gravity acts on each body
No net external force acts on the system
x: Momentum of a system is conserved when it is isolated, i.e. the net external force is zero. Internal forces cancel in pairs by the third law. Kinetic energy need not be conserved.

q: Projectile motion is an example of:
o: Two-dimensional motion in a vertical plane
One-dimensional motion along a straight line
Circular motion in a horizontal plane
x: A projectile moves forward and up or down at the same time, so its motion has a horizontal and a vertical part. Both lie in one vertical plane, which makes it two-dimensional motion.

q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
x: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Distance, speed and time have magnitude only and are scalars.

q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. The distance it covers is:
x: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 2 × 5² = 25 m. 50 m comes from forgetting the factor ½.

q: When a moving bus brakes suddenly, standing passengers tend to fall forward. This is due to:
o: A forward force exerted by the brakes on the passengers
The inertia of motion of their bodies
The reaction force of the floor pushing them forward
Gravity acting more strongly during braking
x: The bus slows, but the passengers' bodies tend to keep moving forward because of inertia (first law). No extra forward force acts on them.

q: Two bodies interact only with each other for a short time. By Newton's third law, the changes in their momenta are:
o: Equal in magnitude and in the same direction
Unequal, the lighter body changing more
Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
x: The bodies exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so the impulses (F × t) are equal and opposite. Hence the momentum changes cancel and total momentum is conserved.

q: A ball is thrown at an angle to the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, in which plane does the whole of its motion take place?
o: The horizontal plane through the point of launch
The vertical plane that contains its initial velocity
A plane perpendicular to its initial velocity
A plane that keeps changing during the flight
x: The initial velocity and the only force (weight, acting straight down) both lie in the vertical plane containing the initial velocity. Nothing pushes the ball out of that plane, so it stays in it.

q: An athlete runs exactly one lap of a 400 m circular track and stops at the starting point. The distance covered and the magnitude of the displacement are:
x: The path length is 400 m, but the final position is the same as the initial position, so the displacement is zero.

q: A car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes uniformly and stops in a distance of 40 m. The magnitude of its deceleration is:
x: v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 20² − 2a × 40, so a = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m s⁻². 10 m s⁻² comes from forgetting the factor 2.

q: A car moves at a steady 20 m s⁻¹ along a straight, level road with its engine running. The net force on the car is:
o: Equal to the forward force of the engine
Equal to the weight of the car
x: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Newton's first and second laws the net force is zero: the forward driving force is balanced by friction and air resistance.

q: The total momentum of an isolated system of two bodies is 10 kg m s⁻¹ due east. After the bodies push on each other, the total momentum of the system is:
x: Internal forces are third-law pairs and cancel, so with no external force the total momentum remains unchanged in size and direction: 10 kg m s⁻¹ east.

q: Why is the motion of a projectile two-dimensional rather than three-dimensional?
o: Its horizontal velocity is zero throughout the flight
Its initial velocity and its weight lie in one vertical plane, so no sideways velocity develops
Air resistance keeps it moving in a single plane
Gravity acts horizontally and cancels any sideways motion
x: With no force acting perpendicular to the vertical plane of launch, no velocity component can develop in that direction. Gravity acts vertically, not horizontally, and the horizontal velocity is not zero.

q: A boy walks 3 m due east and then 4 m due north. The magnitude of his displacement is:
x: The two legs are at right angles, so displacement = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 m. 7 m is the distance travelled, not the displacement.

q: A stone is dropped from rest from a tall tower. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its velocity after 3 s is:
x: v = u + gt = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m s⁻¹. 45 is the distance fallen in metres (½ × 10 × 3²), not the velocity.

q: A 50 kg person stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m s⁻². Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the reading of the scale is:
x: R − mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 50 × (10 + 2) = 600 N. 400 N would be for a lift accelerating downward.

q: In an inelastic collision between two bodies, with no external force:
o: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not
Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
x: Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy turns into heat, sound or deformation.

q: The motion of a projectile can be treated as a combination of:
o: Uniform acceleration horizontally and uniform velocity vertically
Uniform velocity horizontally and uniform acceleration vertically
Uniform velocity both horizontally and vertically
Uniform acceleration both horizontally and vertically
x: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity is constant. Vertically the weight gives a constant acceleration g downward.

q: A particle moves along a semicircle of radius 7 m from one end of a diameter to the other. Taking π = 22/7, the ratio of distance travelled to magnitude of displacement is:
x: Distance = πr = 22 m; displacement = diameter = 14 m. Ratio 22 : 14 = 11 : 7.

q: The equations of motion v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as can be used only when the body moves in a straight line with:
x: These equations are derived assuming the acceleration is constant. For variable acceleration they do not apply.

q: A 50 kg person stands on a scale in a lift moving downward at a constant velocity. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the scale reads:
x: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the normal reaction equals the weight: R = mg = 50 × 10 = 500 N. The direction of motion does not matter, only the acceleration.

q: A collision is called perfectly inelastic when the colliding bodies:
o: Stick together and move with a common velocity
Bounce apart with no loss of kinetic energy
Come to rest without any change in momentum
x: In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together, so they move with one common velocity; the loss of kinetic energy is the maximum possible while momentum is conserved.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of projectile motion?
o: A football kicked up into the air
A car moving round a circular track at constant speed
A bullet fired horizontally from the top of a cliff
A javelin thrown by an athlete
x: A projectile moves freely under gravity alone after launch. The car is kept on a circular path by friction from the road in a horizontal plane, so it is not a projectile.

q: Which statement about distance and displacement is correct?
o: Distance can be negative if the body moves backwards
Displacement always equals the distance travelled
The magnitude of displacement can never be greater than the distance travelled
Displacement depends on the actual path taken between two points
x: The straight line between two points is the shortest path, so |displacement| ≤ distance. Displacement depends only on the start and end points, not on the path; distance is never negative.

q: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration. The distances it covers in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds are in the ratio:
x: Total distances after 1, 2, 3 s are proportional to 1, 4, 9 (s = ½at²). Distances in each separate second are 1, 4 − 1, 9 − 4 = 1 : 3 : 5. 1 : 4 : 9 is the ratio of total distances.

q: The cable of a lift breaks and the lift falls freely. A person standing on a weighing scale inside the lift would read:
x: In free fall the lift's acceleration is g downward, so R = m(g − a) = m(g − g) = 0: the person is apparently weightless.

q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides with a 1 kg trolley at rest, and they stick together. Their common velocity is:
x: Momentum: 2 × 6 + 1 × 0 = (2 + 1)v, so v = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m s⁻¹. 3 m s⁻¹ would be the simple average of 6 and 0.

q: To give the position of a projectile at any instant, relative to its point of launch, you need:
o: Its horizontal distance and its vertical height
Its horizontal distance, its height and a sideways distance
x: The motion lies in one vertical plane, so two coordinates (x horizontally and y vertically) fix the position. No sideways coordinate is needed because there is no sideways motion.

q: A particle on the x-axis moves from x = +3 m to x = −5 m. Its displacement is:
x: Displacement = final position − initial position = (−5) − (+3) = −8 m, i.e. 8 m in the negative x-direction.

q: A car starts from rest with uniform acceleration and covers 20 m in the first 2 s. The total distance it covers in the first 4 s is:
x: From rest, s = ½at², so s ∝ t². Doubling the time multiplies the distance by 4: 4 × 20 = 80 m. 40 m wrongly assumes s ∝ t.

q: A block slides down a smooth (frictionless) plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and sin 30° = 0.5, its acceleration down the plane is:
x: The component of weight along the plane is mg sin θ, so a = g sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m s⁻². 8.7 m s⁻² wrongly uses g cos 30°.

q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides with a 1 kg trolley at rest and they move off together at 4 m s⁻¹. The kinetic energy lost in the collision is:
x: KE before = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J; KE after = ½ × 3 × 4² = 24 J. Loss = 36 − 24 = 12 J. Zero would only be true for an elastic collision.

q: A ball is launched from the ground with speed v at an angle θ above the horizontal. For which value of θ is its motion one-dimensional instead of two-dimensional?
x: At 90° the ball has no horizontal component of velocity (cos 90° = 0), so it simply goes straight up and comes straight down. At any of the other angles it has both components and moves in two dimensions.

q: The velocity–time graph of a car is a straight line rising from 4 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 16 m s⁻¹ at t = 6 s. The acceleration of the car is:
x: Acceleration is the slope of the v–t graph: (16 − 4) ÷ 6 = 2 m s⁻². Dividing the final velocity alone by the time gives about 2.7 m s⁻², and 12 is only the change in velocity.

q: The velocity–time graph of a body is a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 12 m s⁻¹ at t = 4 s, and then a horizontal line at 12 m s⁻¹ until t = 10 s. The distance covered in the 10 s is:
x: Distance = area under the v–t graph: triangle ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m plus rectangle 6 × 12 = 72 m, total 96 m. Using 12 m s⁻¹ for the whole 10 s gives 120 m; taking the whole graph as one triangle gives 60 m.

q: A car covers the first half of a straight journey at 40 km h⁻¹ and the second half of the same distance at 60 km h⁻¹. Its average speed for the whole journey is:
x: For a total distance 2d: time = d/40 + d/60 = 5d/120 = d/24, so average speed = 2d ÷ (d/24) = 48 km h⁻¹. The simple average 50 km h⁻¹ is wrong because the car spends more time at the lower speed.

q: The slope of a displacement–time graph gives the body's:
x: Slope = change in displacement ÷ time = velocity. The slope of a velocity–time graph, not a displacement–time graph, gives acceleration.

q: A body moving at 2 m s⁻¹ has a constant acceleration of 3 m s⁻² in its direction of motion for 4 s. Using the area under its acceleration–time graph, its final velocity is:
x: Area under the a–t graph = change in velocity = 3 × 4 = 12 m s⁻¹, so v = 2 + 12 = 14 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the initial velocity gives 12 m s⁻¹.

q: A body moves in the negative x-direction, and its acceleration is also in the negative x-direction. Its speed is:
x: When velocity and acceleration point the same way, the speed increases, whatever the sign. A negative acceleration means slowing down only when it is opposite to the velocity.

q: A ball's velocity changes from 10 m s⁻¹ due east to 10 m s⁻¹ due west in 4 s. Its average acceleration is:
x: Taking east as positive, Δv = (−10) − (+10) = −20 m s⁻¹, so a = −20 ÷ 4 = −5 m s⁻², i.e. 5 m s⁻² due west. Subtracting speeds instead of velocities gives zero.

q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the greatest height it reaches is:
x: At the top v = 0, so 0 = u² − 2gh gives h = u²/2g = 400 ÷ 20 = 20 m. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 40 m.

q: A stone is thrown vertically upward at 15 m s⁻¹ and caught at the same height. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the total time it is in the air is:
x: Time to the top = u/g = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 s, and the fall back takes the same time, so 3 s in all. 1.5 s is only the upward part.

q: A stone is thrown vertically downward at 5 m s⁻¹ from the top of a building 30 m high. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed just before it hits the ground is:
x: v² = u² + 2gh = 25 + 600 = 625, so v = 25 m s⁻¹. Check: 30 = 5t + 5t² gives t = 2 s and v = 5 + 10 × 2 = 25 m s⁻¹. Leaving out the initial 5 m s⁻¹ gives √600 = 10√6 m s⁻¹.

q: A body has an initial velocity of 2 m s⁻¹ and a uniform acceleration of 4 m s⁻². The distance it covers during the 3rd second alone is:
x: s(3 s) = 2 × 3 + ½ × 4 × 9 = 24 m and s(2 s) = 2 × 2 + ½ × 4 × 4 = 12 m, so the 3rd second covers 24 − 12 = 12 m (also u + a(n − ½) = 2 + 4 × 2.5). 24 m is the total for 3 s.

q: A car moving at 10 m s⁻¹ stops in 8 m when its brakes are applied. With the same braking deceleration, the stopping distance at 20 m s⁻¹ is:
x: From v² = u² − 2as with v = 0, s = u²/2a, so s ∝ u². Doubling the speed multiplies the distance by 4: 4 × 8 = 32 m. Assuming s ∝ u gives 16 m.

q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m s⁻² for 10 s. It then brakes with a uniform deceleration of 4 m s⁻² until it stops. The total distance it covers is:
x: First stage: v = 2 × 10 = 20 m s⁻¹ and s₁ = ½ × 2 × 10² = 100 m. Braking: s₂ = v²/2a = 400 ÷ 8 = 50 m. Total 150 m. Using 2 m s⁻² for the braking too gives 200 m; 100 m is the first stage only.

q: A 1 kg ball and a 5 kg ball are dropped together from the same height in a vacuum. Which statement is correct?
o: The 5 kg ball has five times the acceleration
They fall with the same acceleration and land together
The 5 kg ball lands first because its weight is larger
x: In free fall every body has the same acceleration g, whatever its mass: the larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass. So both land at the same time.

q: Blocks X (3 kg) and Y (2 kg) are in contact on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force of 10 N pushes X, which in turn pushes Y. The force that X exerts on Y is:
x: Both blocks share the acceleration a = 10 ÷ (3 + 2) = 2 m s⁻². Y needs F = 2 kg × 2 m s⁻² = 4 N. 6 N is the net force on X, and 10 N assumes the whole force passes to Y.

q: The SI unit of impulse, N s, is equivalent to the unit of:
x: 1 N s = 1 kg m s⁻² × 1 s = 1 kg m s⁻¹, the unit of momentum; this matches impulse = change in momentum.

q: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and rebounds straight back at 10 m s⁻¹. The magnitude of the impulse given to the ball by the wall is:
x: Impulse = Δp = m(v − u) = 0.2 × (−10 − 10) = −4 N s, magnitude 4 N s. Forgetting that the velocity reverses gives 0, and using only one velocity gives 2 N s.

q: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang at the two ends of a light string over a smooth, light pulley and are released. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the tension in the string is:
x: a = (3 − 2)g/(3 + 2) = 2 m s⁻². For the 2 kg mass moving up: T = m(g + a) = 2 × 12 = 24 N; check with the 3 kg mass: 3 × (10 − 2) = 24 N. 20 N and 30 N are the two weights.

q: The momentum of a body increases steadily from 10 kg m s⁻¹ to 30 kg m s⁻¹ in 4 s. The net force acting on it is:
x: F = Δp/Δt = (30 − 10) ÷ 4 = 5 N. Using only the final momentum gives 7.5 N, and adding the momenta gives 10 N.

q: An apple of mass 0.1 kg falls freely towards the Earth. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the gravitational force the apple exerts on the Earth is:
x: The Earth pulls the apple down with 0.1 × 10 = 1 N; by Newton's third law the apple pulls the Earth with an equal 1 N in the opposite direction, upward toward the apple. 1 N downward is the force on the apple.

q: According to Newton's second law, the net force on a body is equal to its:
x: F = Δp/Δt, the rate of change of momentum; for constant mass this becomes F = ma. The change of momentum itself is the impulse, F × t.

q: A 2 kg ball X moving at 5 m s⁻¹ makes a head-on elastic collision with an identical ball Y at rest. Just after the collision, the velocities of X and Y are:
x: For equal masses in a head-on elastic collision the velocities are exchanged: X stops and Y moves at 5 m s⁻¹. This conserves both momentum (10 kg m s⁻¹) and KE (25 J); 2.5 m s⁻¹ each conserves momentum but loses KE.

q: A 1 kg ball moving at 6 m s⁻¹ makes a head-on elastic collision with a 2 kg ball at rest. The velocity of the 2 kg ball after the collision is:
x: v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) = 2 × 1 × 6 ÷ 3 = 4 m s⁻¹, and the 1 kg ball rebounds at 2 m s⁻¹. Check: momentum 6 = −2 + 8, KE 18 J = 2 J + 16 J. 2 m s⁻¹ is the common speed if they stuck together.

q: A 4 kg gun at rest fires a 20 g bullet horizontally at 400 m s⁻¹. The recoil speed of the gun is:
x: Total momentum stays zero: 0.02 × 400 = 4 × V, so V = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m s⁻¹. Using 20 kg for the bullet's mass instead of 0.02 kg gives 2000 m s⁻¹.

q: In a head-on elastic collision between two bodies, the relative speed with which they separate is:
o: Equal to the relative speed with which they approached
Half the relative speed of approach
Twice the relative speed of approach
x: For an elastic collision, conservation of momentum and of kinetic energy together give u₁ − u₂ = v₂ − v₁: speed of separation equals speed of approach. Zero separation speed would mean the bodies stick together.

q: A small, light ball makes a head-on elastic collision with a very heavy body at rest. After the collision the light ball:
o: Bounces back with almost the same speed
Moves on with almost the same speed in its original direction
x: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂); with m₂ much greater than m₁, v₁ ≈ −u, so the light ball rebounds with nearly its original speed while the heavy body hardly moves. Stopping dead happens only for equal masses.

q: A 3 kg body at rest explodes into two pieces of 1 kg and 2 kg. The 1 kg piece moves off at 8 m s⁻¹. The total kinetic energy released in the explosion is:
x: Momentum stays zero: 1 × 8 = 2 × v, so v = 4 m s⁻¹. KE = ½ × 1 × 8² + ½ × 2 × 4² = 32 + 16 = 48 J. 32 J counts only the 1 kg piece; dropping the ½ gives 96 J.

q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m s⁻¹ due east collides head-on with a 1 kg trolley moving at 3 m s⁻¹ due west. They stick together. Their common velocity is:
x: Taking east as positive: 2 × 3 + 1 × (−3) = 3v, so v = 3 ÷ 3 = 1 m s⁻¹ east. Treating both velocities as positive gives 9 ÷ 3 = 3 m s⁻¹.

q: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ at 45° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its horizontal range is:
x: R = u² sin 2θ/g = 400 × sin 90° ÷ 10 = 40 m. Dividing by 2g gives 20 m, and forgetting to divide by g gives 400 m.

q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal (sin 30° = 0.5). Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the maximum height it reaches is:
x: H = u² sin²θ/2g = 400 × 0.25 ÷ 20 = 5 m. Not squaring sin 30° gives 10 m, using cos²30° gives 15 m, and 20 m is the height for a vertical throw.

q: A projectile is launched from level ground at 30 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal (sin 30° = 0.5). Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its time of flight is:
x: T = 2u sin θ/g = 2 × 30 × 0.5 ÷ 10 = 3 s. 1.5 s is only the time to the highest point, and using cos 30° gives about 5.2 s.

q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff 45 m high. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², it lands at a horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff of:
x: Vertically from rest: 45 = ½ × 10 × t², so t = 3 s. Horizontally x = 10 × 3 = 30 m. Using t² = 9 in place of t gives 90 m, and 45 m simply repeats the height.

q: Ignoring air resistance, the acceleration of a projectile at the highest point of its path is:
o: Less than g, because its vertical velocity is zero
x: The only force on the projectile is its weight throughout the flight, so its acceleration is always g downward. At the top only the vertical velocity is zero, not the acceleration.

q: Two balls are projected from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, the ratio of their maximum heights (30° : 60°) is:
x: H = u² sin²θ/2g, so H ∝ sin²θ: sin²30° : sin²60° = ¼ : ¾ = 1 : 3. Not squaring the sines gives 1 : √3; their ranges, by contrast, are equal.

q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed just before it hits the ground is:
x: Fall time: 20 = 5t², t = 2 s, so vy = 20 m s⁻¹ and vx stays 15 m s⁻¹. Speed = √(15² + 20²) = 25 m s⁻¹; energy check: v² = 225 + 2 × 10 × 20 = 625. Adding the components gives 35 m s⁻¹.
